lesson.title: When Fear of France Collided with the First Amendment
lesson.summary: Passed in 1798 amid war fears sparked by the XYZ Affair, the Alien and Sedition Acts restricted immigrants and criminalized criticism of the government, provoking a backlash over their conflict with the Bill of Rights.
lesson.body:
In the summer of 1798, with the United States and France locked in the undeclared naval conflict known as the Quasi War and the shock of the XYZ Affair still fresh, the Federalist controlled Congress passed a series of four laws collectively known as the Alien and Sedition Acts. Federalists argued the laws were necessary for national security, since they suspected recent immigrants and French sympathizers, many of whom supported the opposition Democratic-Republican Party, of posing a real threat of espionage or insurrection.

Three of the laws targeted foreigners. The Naturalization Act extended the residency requirement for citizenship from five years to fourteen, making it far harder for immigrants, who tended to favor Jefferson's party, to gain voting rights. The Alien Friends Act gave the president power to deport any noncitizen deemed dangerous, and the Alien Enemies Act allowed the government to detain or deport citizens of a hostile nation during wartime, a law significant enough that it remained on the books and was invoked again in later American conflicts.

The fourth and most controversial law, the Sedition Act, went well beyond regulating immigrants. It made it a federal crime to publish false, scandalous, or malicious statements against the government, Congress, or the president, with penalties including fines and imprisonment. Notably, the law did not extend the same protection to the vice president, meaning Federalist writers could still attack Jefferson freely even while criticizing Adams became a punishable offense. In practice, Federalist prosecutors used the law almost exclusively against Democratic-Republican newspaper editors and even a sitting congressman, Matthew Lyon of Vermont, who was jailed for criticizing Adams.

Critics argued the Sedition Act directly violated the First Amendment's protection of freedom of speech and the press, one of the core guarantees added to the Constitution in the Bill of Rights less than a decade earlier. Jefferson and Madison, watching from outside the administration, saw the law as proof that the Federalists were willing to use national security fears to silence political opposition and consolidate power, a fear that echoed the concerns Jefferson had raised years earlier as Secretary of State about how far federal authority could stretch.

The backlash proved significant. Rather than crushing the Democratic-Republicans, the Sedition Act turned prosecuted editors into political martyrs and helped convince many Americans that the Federalists had overreached. Jefferson and Madison responded by secretly drafting the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions, arguing that states had the right to judge the constitutionality of federal laws, and the resulting public anger over the acts became one of the central issues Jefferson's supporters used against Adams in the election of 1800, contributing directly to the Federalist defeat.
